title: Introduction to quantum physics
summary: Blackbody, photon, photoelectric effect, Compton, de Broglie and the Bohr model.
cards.0.p: Every object radiates. An ideal object that absorbs all the light falling on it is called a blackbody. As temperature rises, the radiation grows and the peak wavelength gets shorter: λmax·T ≈ 2.9×10⁻³ m·K.
cards.0.key: Every object above absolute zero radiates. Heated iron glows red first, then close to white. The Sun radiates in the visible, and you radiate in the infrared.
cards.1.p: Classical physics predicted that radiation would grow without limit at short wavelengths. But the experiments did not show this. In 1900 Planck proposed that energy is exchanged in packets called quanta: E = n·h·f.
cards.1.key: h ≈ 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant. Energy can change only by whole multiples of h·f.
cards.1.once.soru: According to Planck, how does a light source give off energy?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: Energy is exchanged in packets of size h·f.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: Classical physics thought so, but this idea did not agree with experiment.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: The source radiates continuously, but its energy changes packet by packet.
cards.2.p: Light is made of packets called photons. The energy of a photon is E = h·f = h·c/λ. At the atomic scale the unit electronvolt is used: E(eV) ≈ 1240 / λ(nm).
cards.2.key: 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J. The shorter the wavelength, the greater the photon energy.
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: The photon with the shorter wavelength has more energy: 1240/400 ≈ 3.1 eV.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: The energy of the red photon is 1240/700 ≈ 1.8 eV.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.
cards.3.h: The photoelectric effect and the threshold
cards.3.p: When light falling on a metal knocks out electrons, this is called the photoelectric effect. The smallest energy needed for this is called the work function: W = h·f0. If f < f0, no electron comes out.
cards.3.key: f₀ is the threshold frequency, and W is also called the binding energy. Frequency sets the threshold. Intensity or waiting time does not.
cards.4.p: An electron absorbs a single photon. An amount W of the energy goes into freeing the electron, and the rest becomes kinetic energy: Ek,max = h·f − W. Electrons from deeper in the metal come out slower.
cards.4.key: As f increases, the maximum kinetic energy increases too, but it is not directly proportional to f, because W is subtracted.
cards.4.etk.soru: Change the wavelength of the light and the work function of the metal. E(eV) ≈ 1240 / λ(nm).
cards.4.etk.yorum.0.1: No electron is ejected, because the photon energy is less than W (f < f<sub>0</sub>). Raising the intensity does not help either.
cards.4.etk.yorum.1.1: This is exactly the threshold (f = f<sub>0</sub>), and the photon energy equals W. The electron barely gets out and its kinetic energy is zero.
cards.4.etk.yorum.2.1: The electron is ejected, but it comes out very slowly. The photon energy is only slightly above W, and the small extra energy becomes kinetic energy.
cards.4.etk.yorum.3.1: The electron is ejected, because the photon energy is greater than W. The extra energy becomes kinetic energy.
cards.5.p: When intensity rises, more photons arrive each second and more electrons are ejected. So the saturation current rises, but Ek,max does not change. For the stopping voltage, e·V0 = Ek,max.
cards.5.key: Intensity changes the current. V₀ is set only by the frequency of the light and the kind of metal.
cards.6.p: The graph of Ek,max against frequency is a straight line. Its slope is h, the same for every metal. The line crosses the f axis at the threshold frequency f0.
cards.6.key: Extended backward, the line crosses the vertical axis at −W. The lines for different metals are parallel.
cards.6.once.soru: The Ek,max–frequency graph is drawn for two different metals. How do the slopes of the lines compare?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: The slope is Planck's constant h and does not depend on the metal.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: W only shifts the line to the right. It does not change the slope.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The slope is h for every metal.
cards.7.p: In a Compton collision, energy and momentum are conserved. A photon has no mass, but it has momentum: p = h/λ. Since the electron takes energy, the wavelength of the scattered photon gets longer.
cards.7.key: The Compton effect shows that light collides like a particle.
cards.8.p: According to de Broglie, every particle has a wavelength: λ = h/(m·v). Electrons sent at a crystal formed a diffraction pattern, just like light. The wavelength of a ball is far too small to measure.
cards.8.key: de Broglie proposed this in 1924, and experiment confirmed it in 1927. The greater the mass or speed, the shorter the wavelength.
cards.9.p: Light and electrons sometimes behave like waves and sometimes like particles. This is called wave-particle duality. By the uncertainty principle, position and momentum cannot both be known exactly at the same time: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π.
cards.9.svg#9: position and momentum cannot both be known exactly
cards.9.key: The Compton effect is also particle behavior. Uncertainty is not a flaw of the measuring device. It is a basic property of nature.
cards.9.once.soru: In which event does light behave like a particle?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: A single photon ejects a single electron. This is particle behavior.
cards.10.p: According to Bohr, the electron in hydrogen moves only in certain stable orbits and does not radiate while in them. The energy of the levels is En = −13.6/n² eV.
cards.10.key: The minus sign shows that the electron is bound to the atom. Ionizing an atom at n = 1 takes 13.6 eV. This model works only for atoms with one electron.
cards.10.once.soru: In hydrogen, Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. What is E₂?
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: You divide by n², not by n.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: Here it was multiplied instead of divided. It should be −13.6 / 4.
cards.11.p: When an electron drops from an upper level to a lower one, it emits the energy difference as a single photon: h·f = Eupper − Elower. A heated gas gives emission lines, and a cold gas gives absorption lines.
cards.11.key: When white light passes through a cold gas, the same wavelengths are absorbed. The lines of each element are like a fingerprint.
cards.12.h: Two ways to excite an atom
cards.12.p: A photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly equals the difference between two levels. A colliding electron excites the atom if it arrives with energy equal to or greater than the difference, and moves on with the rest.
cards.12.key: A photon above the ionization energy (13.6 eV in hydrogen) is absorbed, though. The extra energy goes to the freed electron.
cards.12.once.soru: In hydrogen the first excitation takes 10.2 eV and the second 12.1 eV. What happens if an 11 eV photon arrives?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: A photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly equals a level difference.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: A photon cannot split its energy and leave the extra behind.
cards.13.h: From Bohr to the modern atomic model
cards.13.p: The Bohr model could not explain atoms with many electrons. In the modern model the electron does not move in a definite orbit, and only the probability of finding it is known. A region where the probability is high is called an orbital.
cards.13.key: The energy levels are still quantized. You will see orbital types and filling order in the Chemistry topic Modern atomic theory.
cards.13.once.soru: In the modern atomic model, what is known about where the electron is?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Because of the uncertainty principle, only where it may be found is known.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: An exact orbit belonged to the Bohr model.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: The regions where the probability is high (orbitals) are known.
cards.14.p: A solar cell produces current from photon energy, a photocell detects light, and an LED emits photons. A laser produces a narrow beam of one color with all waves in phase.
cards.14.key: Photocells also control streetlights. A laser works by stimulated emission. The energy gap sets the color of an LED.
cards.14.once.soru: An automatic door detects a person passing when a light beam is cut. Which device is used?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: While light falls on the photocell, current flows. When the light is cut, the door opens.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: A magnet does not detect light.
cards.15.p:
• Energy is quantized: E = h·f = h·c/λ.
• In the photoelectric effect, Ek,max = h·f − W = e·V0.
• Intensity changes only the current.
• For a photon p = h/λ, and for a matter wave λ = h/(m·v).
• In hydrogen, En = −13.6/n² eV.
quiz.0.q: Light of wavelength 310 nm falls on a metal whose work function is 2 eV. What voltage stops the ejected electrons (the stopping voltage), in volts? (h·c ≈ 1240 eV·nm)
quiz.0.e: The photon energy is 1240/310 = 4 eV. E<sub>k,max</sub> = 4 − 2 = 2 eV. Since e·V<sub>0</sub> = E<sub>k,max</sub>, V<sub>0</sub> = 2 V.
quiz.1.q: Only the intensity of light above the threshold frequency is increased. What happens to each quantity?
quiz.1.e: Intensity raises the number of photons arriving each second. More electrons are ejected and the current grows. Since the energy of each photon (h·f) stays the same, E<sub>k,max</sub> and the stopping voltage do not change. The threshold frequency depends on the metal.
quiz.2.q: Match each scientist with their contribution.
quiz.2.ciftler.0.1: Energy is exchanged in quantum packets
quiz.2.ciftler.1.1: The scattered photon's wavelength gets longer
quiz.2.e: Planck showed that energy is exchanged in packets, and Compton that the wavelength of a scattered X-ray gets longer. de Broglie gave particles a wavelength, Heisenberg put forward the uncertainty principle, and Bohr the energy levels of hydrogen.
quiz.3.q: In the E<sub>k,max</sub>–f graph drawn for metals K and L, the two lines are parallel and L's line crosses the f axis at a higher frequency. Which is true?
quiz.3.o.0: L's line has a greater slope.
quiz.3.o.1: K has the higher threshold frequency.
quiz.3.o.2: For light of the same frequency, electrons from L have a greater E<sub>k,max</sub>.
quiz.3.o.3: L has the greater work function.
quiz.3.e: A metal with a higher threshold frequency also has a greater work function (W = h·f<sub>0</sub>). The slope is h for both metals. At the same f, L, with the greater W, has the smaller E<sub>k,max</sub>.
quiz.3.y.0: The slope of the lines equals Planck's constant. Since the lines are parallel, their slopes are the same.
quiz.3.y.1: The point where a line crosses the f axis is the threshold frequency. The higher threshold frequency belongs to L.
quiz.3.y.2: Electrons from L, which has the greater work function, come out with less energy. So E<sub>k,max</sub> is smaller.
A:ozet: Heat the object and change its color. Try to eject electrons from a metal, find the stopping voltage and raise the intensity. Scatter an X-ray, send electrons through a double slit and find the color of hydrogen.
A:adimlar.0.metin: By Wien's law, λmax·T ≈ 2.9·10⁶ nm·K. Set the temperature so that the peak of the curve is at 500 nm.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: By Wien's law, λmax = 2.9·10⁶ / 5800 = 500 nm. This is the surface temperature of the Sun.
A:adimlar.1.metin: When light falls on a metal, electrons can be ejected. Ejecting an electron from sodium takes at least W = 2.3 eV. Change the color and the intensity, and make at least two different tries.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: What decides whether an electron is ejected?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Raising the intensity of red light brings more photons, but each still carries less than 2.3 eV.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: An electron absorbs a single photon, and energy does not build up. So waiting below the threshold does not help.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: An electron takes the energy of a single photon (h·f). If h·f < W, no electron comes out however intense the light is. For sodium the threshold is about 540 nm.
A:adimlar.2.metin: The maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron is Ek,max = h·f − W. The photon energy is found with E(eV) ≈ 1240/λ(nm), and for sodium W = 2.3 eV. The reverse voltage that stops the fastest electron is called V0: e·V0 = Ek,max. Set the wavelength so that V0 is 0.8 V.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: At 400 nm the photon energy is 1240/400 = 3.1 eV. Ek,max = 3.1 − 2.3 = 0.8 eV and V0 = 0.8 V.
A:adimlar.3.metin: We shine the same 400 nm light on a sodium plate. In the setup on the right the light has twice the intensity, so twice as many photons arrive each second.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: What happens when the intensity doubles?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The energy of each photon is h·f. Intensity raises the number of photons, not the energy of a photon.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: Current rises, E<sub>k,max</sub> stays the same
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Twice the photons eject twice the electrons, and the current grows. Each electron still takes the energy of a single photon and comes out with at most 0.8 eV.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The current rises, but the energy of the electrons depends on the energy of a single photon.
A:adimlar.4.metin: In 1923 Compton made X-ray photons collide with electrons. A photon has no mass, but it has momentum: p = h/λ. The photon will now hit the electron and scatter.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: What happens to the wavelength of the scattered photon?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The photon gives part of its energy to the electron. Its energy drops, λ grows and f gets smaller. The photon's speed is still c.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A shorter wavelength would mean the photon gained energy. But part of the energy goes to the recoiling electron.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Since the electron recoils, it has taken some energy. That energy comes from the photon.
A:adimlar.5.metin: de Broglie said that every particle has a wavelength: λ = h/(m·v). Now we send electrons one at a time through two slits to a screen.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: What forms on the screen over time?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: That would happen if electrons behaved only like tiny balls. But the waves from the two slits interfere.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: One by one the dots look random. But when thousands build up, a regular pattern appears.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Each electron lands on the screen as a single dot, which is particle behavior. But as the dots build up, interference fringes appear, which is wave behavior. This is called wave-particle duality.
A:adimlar.6.metin: When an electron drops to a lower level, it emits a photon with the energy difference of the two levels. In hydrogen, En = −13.6/n² eV. Find the transition that gives the blue-green photon of 2.55 eV.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: E4 − E2 = −0.85 − (−3.4) = 2.55 eV and λ = 1240/2.55 ≈ 486 nm. Most transitions down to n = 2 are in the visible range and are called the Balmer series. Those down to n = 1 are in the ultraviolet and are called the Lyman series.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.ipucu: The energies of the levels are −13.6, −3.4, −1.51 and −0.85 eV. Look for the pair whose difference is 2.55.
A:kapanis.0: Energy is quantized: E = h·f = h·c/λ. In electronvolts, E(eV) ≈ 1240 / λ(nm).
A:kapanis.1: For a blackbody, the peak wavelength is found with λmax·T ≈ 2.9·10⁻³ m·K.
A:kapanis.2: In the photoelectric effect, Ek,max = h·f − W = e·V₀. Frequency sets the threshold, and intensity changes only the current.
A:kapanis.3: In the Compton effect the photon carries momentum: p = h/λ. The wavelength of the scattered photon gets longer.
A:kapanis.4: The wavelength of a matter wave is found with λ = h/(m·v). Electrons interfere too.
A:kapanis.5: In hydrogen, En = −13.6/n² eV. The emitted photon carries the energy difference between the levels.
